assays.assay_name: Two-choice visual discrimination maze (luminance- and motion-based tasks)
assays.assay_description: Rats performed a 2-choice visual discrimination task in a PVC Y-shaped maze with 2 arms (120°) ending in screens. Two task variants were used: a luminance-based task (black vs. white screens) and a motion-based task (static vertical square-wave gratings vs. dynamic distorted gratings). Correct responses were rewarded with a cornball; incorrect responses produced a 30-s confinement. Outcomes were correct ratio and decision time (time in a predefined decision zone), recorded from above using EthoVision Pro. Testing occurred 30 min after s.c. psilocin (0.3 mg/kg) or saline.

application_type.evidence: Psilocin (0.3 mg/kg) or saline was subcutaneously injected

setup_habituation.evidence: No explicit habituation to the apparatus prior to training is described.

setup_restrain.evidence: Each trial began when the maze door opened, which allowed the rat to enter and choose between 2 screens.

food_restriction.evidence: Food restriction ensured motivation for reward-based learning, with weights maintained above 90% of baseline.

time_to_assay.evidence: Psilocin (0.3 mg/kg) or saline was subcutaneously injected... 30 minutes before testing.

sample_size.evidence: Six rats were tested in both tasks.

outcomes.summary: Psilocin (0.3 mg/kg s.c.) significantly impaired discrimination of static vs. dynamic stimuli in the motion-based task (saline 93.3% vs. psilocin 72.7% correct), but did not significantly impair the luminance-based task, indicating a perceptual rather than general cognitive/motivational deficit. Decision time was inversely correlated with correct ratio.
outcomes.statistics: t11 = 4.693, p < .001 (correct ratio saline vs psilocin); r = -0.440, p < .05 (decision time vs correct ratio); t5 = 4.067, p < .001 (motion- vs luminance-based impairment)
outcomes.evidence: The correct ratio was significantly lower in psilocin trials than in saline trials (dependent Student's t test, t11 = 4.693, p < .001)... Discrimination impairment varied by task complexity, being significantly greater in the motion-based task than the luminance-based task (t5 = 4.067, p < .001).

D1_continuity.evidence: The 3-day testing phase assessed psilocin's effect on visual discrimination. On the first day (baseline)... On the second day, rats received saline... On the third day, psilocin was administered.

D2_session_duration.evidence: Session was 24 testing trials with 30-s penalties; explicit duration not reported but consistent with short sessions.

D3_recording_days.evidence: 3-day testing phase... A posttreatment training session was conducted the following day... After a 1-week washout period, rats were retrained on the luminance task and retested following the same protocol.

D4_baseline.evidence: On the first day (baseline), rats completed 20 training trials followed by 24 testing trials, where incorrect responses were rewarded.

D5_followup.evidence: A posttreatment training session was conducted the following day to verify that psilocin exposure did not impair task retention — this was a training session, not a drug-effect recording; testing of psilocin effect occurred 30 min post-injection only.

D6_circadian.evidence: Sessions are short trial-based blocks, well under 6 h.

judge_notes: Merged candidate glm's two separate assay entries (luminance-based vs. motion-based) into a single visual-discrimination-maze assay, because the same paradigm/apparatus/outcomes are used with only stimulus parameters differing — per rubric, same task with different stimulus parameters = 1 assay.
